title: The Night of Freedom
lead: God can lead people out into freedom after years of slavery.
questions: If God opened the door of your longest captivity today, would you be packed and ready, or have you already made yourself at home in it?
Which of your captivities has become a safe routine and no longer hurts at all?
Whom could you invite under your roof, behind a door marked with blood, the way the Israelites did that night?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: Nine plagues did not open the gates of Egypt. The tenth night did, a night when freedom came not through a battle but through a lamb, a meal, and a sign on the door. It began with a calendar: “This month is the beginning of months for you.” For a slave, time goes around in circles; freedom begins when he is given a new beginning. And God announced it to people who were still slaves, as if the first thing to leave Egypt was meant to be their imagination.

The lamb was “one per household”: the door was the altar, the father of the family served as priest, and anyone whose household was too small shared with a neighbor. The lamb’s blood was put on the doorframes. “The blood shall be to you for a token on the houses where you are: and when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (WEB). To you, because it wasn’t God who needed a sign; people needed to see what their rescue rested on. Not on their ancestry and not on their merits. The one who survived was not the one who was better, but the one who believed the warning and stayed where he was told. The dividing line that night did not run between nations but between those who believed and those who didn’t: “a mixed multitude also went up with them,” and the Passover law from the start treated the foreigner the same as the native-born.

They ate with sandals on and staff in hand, in haste: a meal for people dressed for the road. And in the middle of the night Pharaoh gave in: “Get up, leave my people.” After 430 years, to the very day, the doors opened in a single night. And one sentence remains, perhaps the most tender in the whole book: “the LORD kept a vigil that night to bring them out of the land of Egypt.” No one in Egypt slept that night, but God kept watch the longest. There was also a detail in the instructions that pointed to the future: none of the lamb’s bones were to be broken. Centuries later soldiers did not break the legs of the Crucified One, and He Himself, at the Passover table, applied the words about remembrance to Himself: “do this in remembrance of Me.” The night of freedom turned out to be a sign of a greater freedom.

This reading is for people who have been rooted in something for so long that they have stopped believing there is a way out. God can close an extraordinarily long era very quickly. That night the Lord required only three things of people: to believe the warning, to stay inside the house marked with blood, and to be ready for the road.

From the bush at Horeb to this night is a long, hard road. Pharaoh answered the first message with mockery and heavier work quotas; then came the plagues, one after another, and after each one the ruler’s heart hardened all over again. Nine blows did not open the gates of Egypt. The tenth night opened them, the strangest night in the Old Testament: a night when freedom came not through a battle, not through a slave uprising, but through a lamb, a meal, and blood on the door.

sections.heading: A New Calendar
paragraphs: Chapter 12 begins with something that sounds almost bureaucratic: “This month is the beginning of months for you; it shall be the first month of your year.” God tells Israel to change its calendar. The new year would no longer be counted from the harvest or from the river’s flooding, as with the neighbors, but from the night of freedom. That is a bold statement: a slave counts time from one shift of work to the next, and nothing ever changes. Freedom begins with a new calendar, a new beginning. People in Alcoholics Anonymous count time from the day they broke free of their addiction. Those who have met God count it from their own Passover night. Your calendar reveals what you consider the most important event of your life. And there is one more interesting detail: God announces a new beginning to people who are still slaves. He hands out calendars of freedom before the liberation, as if He wanted the first thing to leave Egypt to be their awareness and their faith.

sections.heading: A Lamb for Every Household
paragraphs: “On the tenth day of this month each man must select a lamb for his family, one per household.” Not a lamb for the temple, because there is no temple. Not for the nation, because for now the nation is a crowd of slaves. For the household. The first sacrifice Israel receives as a people is a home sacrifice: the door is the altar, the father of the family is the priest, the kitchen and the threshold are the sanctuary. And if the family is too small, “they are to share with the nearest neighbor.” Right in the middle of the sacrificial instructions there is a concern that no one be left alone and nothing go to waste. From the very beginning, freedom has the shape of a table where you have to sit down with someone.

The lamb had to be “an unblemished year-old male.” It was chosen on the tenth day and slaughtered on the fourteenth. For four days the animal lived in the house, in front of the children, probably with a name they had already given it. That delay was not cruelty; it was a lesson: rescue has a price, and that price lives with you under one roof before it is paid. Nothing about this night is anonymous.

sections.heading: Blood on the Doorframe
paragraphs: “They are to take some of the blood and put it on the sides and tops of the doorframes of the houses where they eat the lambs.” It was applied with a bunch of hyssop, a roadside herb that grew anywhere and cost nothing. Centuries later someone would lift sour wine to the Crucified One on a stalk of hyssop, a plant hardly suited to the task, but John recorded that detail because he knew which night it connected to. The next sentence is another revelation of God: “The blood shall be to you for a token on the houses where you are: and when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (WEB). A token to you. God didn’t need red paint to tell an Israelite from an Egyptian. People needed to stand before their own door and see what their rescue rested on. Not on who they were, because inside were all kinds of people, brave and cowardly, devout and steeped in Egypt. Not on merit, because that night no one would have had time to earn any. Only on whether the house was marked with the blood of the lamb. The one who survived was not the one who was better. The one who survived was the one who believed the warning and took shelter where he was told.

There is one more detail in these instructions: “None of you shall go out the door of his house until morning.” The sign was on the outside, but it protected those who stayed inside. Blood on the doorframe wasn’t enough if someone decided to step out on his own business. Rescue was a gift, but staying within its bounds was a decision that had to be held onto all night long.

sections.heading: Judgment on the Gods of Egypt
paragraphs: In announcing that night, God says one more sentence: “I will execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt. I am the LORD.” The plagues were not random disasters. Many of them struck at things Egypt worshiped: the Nile, the sun, and finally the house of Pharaoh, who was himself honored as divine. Egypt was a deeply religious superpower: temples at every turn, processions and incantations as part of daily life, and a whole army of intermediaries between heaven and earth. That night it became clear that none of those gods could hold back the judgment of the LORD. Slavery always has its gods, the ones that keep it in place and are served out of fear or habit. Freedom begins when judgment falls on them and it comes to light that they have no power.

sections.heading: Who Went Out That Night
paragraphs: It’s easy to read this story like a sports match: Israel versus Egypt, us versus them. God’s Word is more careful. Earlier, during the plague of hail, Egypt had already split between those who disregarded the warning and those who took it seriously and brought their servants and livestock to shelter. Later, as Israel left, “a mixed multitude also went up with them.” The text doesn’t explain exactly who they were, but it shows that people from outside the nation itself went out along with Israel. The Passover law made room from the start for the foreigner who wanted to take part in the celebration on the same terms. That’s worth remembering the next time we divide the world into the household of God and everyone else: on the night of freedom, the line was not simply the border between Egyptians and Israelites. It ran between believers and unbelievers in both nations.

sections.heading: In Haste, Staff in Hand
paragraphs: The instructions even covered what to wear: “You must be fully dressed for travel, with your sandals on your feet and your staff in your hand. You are to eat in haste.” This is a meal for people dressed for the road. They were to eat their rescue with their shoes on, ready to get up from the table in mid-sentence. Freedom you don’t step out to meet slips away; Egypt knows countless ways to keep a person for just one more night. The dough had no time to rise, and they took it with them just as it was. And then came what four generations had waited for: a cry in the night, Pharaoh summoning Moses in the dark, and words that, coming from this ruler, amount to surrender: “Get up, leave my people… Go, worship the LORD as you have requested.” After years of slavery, the doors opened in a single night. Not because the slaves had grown strong. Because God had passed through Egypt.

And one more thing: they did not leave empty-handed. The Israelites “asked the Egyptians for articles of silver and gold, and for clothing. And the LORD gave the people such favor in the sight of the Egyptians that they granted their request.” Centuries earlier God had told Abraham that his descendants would come out of the house of slavery with great possessions, and the Law would later require every freed slave to be sent off the same way: not empty-handed. A person coming out of slavery is not meant to begin freedom in poverty. God remembered a promise made four generations earlier and kept it down to the last dish.

sections.heading: The Night God Kept Watch
paragraphs: At the end of the chapter the narrator marks the time with striking precision: “At the end of the 430 years, to the very day, all the LORD’s divisions went out of the land of Egypt.” To the very day. Not around then, not more or less. From an earthly point of view, 430 years looked like an eternity with no end date, and it turned out to be a stretch with a precisely fixed end. And right after that comes what may be the most tender sentence in the whole book: “the LORD kept a vigil that night to bring them out of the land of Egypt.” Kept a vigil. Like a parent at the door of a room where the children are sleeping before a long journey. No one in Egypt slept that night, but God stayed awake the longest. And that is why, the Bible says, “this same night is to be a vigil to the LORD, to be observed by all the Israelites for the generations to come.” The answer to the night when the Lord kept watch over people is every night when people keep watch for God. Passover was to be repeated every year as “a memorial,” and when children asked what the ceremony meant, the father was to tell about that night as though he himself were coming out of Egypt. This memorial was not mere remembering. It was stepping into the event anew, every year, with each generation taking part personally.

sections.heading: A Lamb Whose Bones Were Not Broken
paragraphs: The Passover instructions contained a small detail that for centuries looked like culinary fussiness: “you may not break any of the bones.” Centuries later, on a Friday afternoon before the Passover feast, soldiers broke the legs of condemned men to hasten their death before sunset. They didn’t do it to Jesus of Nazareth, because He was already dead. The Gospel writer recorded this and added that it happened so that Scripture would be fulfilled. John the Baptist had earlier called Him the Lamb of God, and He Himself, at the Last Supper, a Passover meal, took the words about remembrance from this chapter and turned them toward Himself: “do this in remembrance of Me.” The night of freedom from Egypt turned out to be a sign of a greater freedom. And once again everything fits: rescue not by our own strength, a house marked with the blood of the Lamb, a table at which no one should be left alone.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: This reading is for people who have been rooted in something for so long that they have stopped believing there is a way out. After years, captivity doesn’t hurt the way it did at first; it becomes a safe routine, a daily schedule, an identity. Israel’s Egypt lasted so long that no one alive remembered freedom. And yet the way opened in a single night. Not when the slaves had gathered their strength, but when they did what God told them to do, even though it looked rather unimpressive: a meal, a sign on the door, bags packed. The hope in this story is not that tomorrow will be better. It is that God can close a very long era very quickly, and that on His side, preparations for your departure are already underway. That night God expected three things of people: to believe the warning, to stay inside the house marked with blood, and to be ready for the road.
